newsitem.title: USA: Dollar ends mixed in U.S. after late rally fizzles.
newsitem.headline: Dollar ends mixed in U.S. after late rally fizzles.

text.p: The dollar retreated from a two-year high against the mark as investors booked profits on the failure to breach resistance at 1.58, traders said.
But the greenback remained comfortably above 1.57 marks, bolstered by a late announcement that Russian President Boris Yeltsin had been hospitalized, apparently with pneumonia.

The greenback peaked at 1.5787 marks after the report from the Kremlin, but shortly slipped below a key technical pivot at 1.5750. The dollar also reached a fresh a 30-month peak against the Swiss franc as investors unloaded European currencies in favor of the more stable U.S. unit.
"The dollar is extremely well bid. This thing with Yeltsin has people getting out of Germany," said Jay Wertheimer, senior currency trader at Banco di Sicilia in New York.

Yeltsin had quintuple bypass surgery in November and the specter of political instability in former Communist Russia sparked mark selling. Germany is Russia's largest trading partner and its economy could suffer if Yeltsin were replaced with a less friendly leader.
The dollar closed at 1.5747/52, up from 1.5725/35 at the open and 1.5640/45 at Tuesday's close. The U.S. unit also rose to 1.3640/50 Swiss francs from 1.3595/05.
Asian and European markets had already pushed the dollar higher early in the session amid broad expectations that a report due Thursday would show record unemployment in Germany.
Also on Thursday, Germany's central bank, the Bundesbank, will conduct a regular fortnightly council meeting, which some analysts speculated might produce a cut in official German interest rates.
"There may be some opportunity for the dollar to score further gains if we get a particularly bad employment report out of Germany," said Lisa Finstrom, currency analyst at Smith Barney.
Weakness in Europe, as well as Japan, contrasts starkly with the U.S. economy, which is growing steadily and attracting the lion's share of investment flows.
Despite a sharp decline in U.S. stock prices Wednesday, traders predicted the market would soon resume its recent trend toward record highs, bolstering the dollar.
"There's still a very positive feeling about U.S. assets and the dollar," said Wertheimer.
Against the yen, the dollar held to narrow ranges after an overnight rebound from two days of heavy selling.
Traders noted Japanese officials fell silent after several had made comments earlier this week calling for a halt to the dollar's recent rally.
"The fact that we did not get another round of verbal intervention from the Japanese may have given speculators a little leeway to test the (yen's) downside," Finstrom said.
The dollar ended lower at 115.77/87 yen versus 115.85/90 at the open, but up from 115.23/28 at Tuesday's close.
Elsewhere, the dollar fell to Canadian $1.3515/20 from C$1.3543/48.
The Bank of Canada appeared to have intervened in the the market to sell the Canadian currency, which has risen sharply of late.
The British pound rose to $1.6875/85 from $1.6868/75 at the open. The Australian dollar fell to $0.7797/02 from $0.7815/25.
((--Chris Stetkiewicz, 212-859-1664))
